title: The Accounting Profession in Australia: Economic Impact and Workforce Outlook
gist: Oxford Economics Australia estimates the accounting profession contributed A$82.4bn (about 3% of GDP) and supported over 365,000 jobs in 2024-25, with the workforce projected to grow ~20% by 2035 yet still leave a shortfall of 17,900 accounting, audit and finance professionals, driven by falling enrolments, attrition, migration constraints and AI's changing role.

insights.claim: Australia's accounting profession contributed A$82.4 billion to national GDP in 2024-25, equivalent to roughly 3% of the Australian economy, per Oxford Economics Australia's analysis commissioned by Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
entities: Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand
insights.so_what: A profession worth ~3% of GDP is a reliable proxy for broader corporate compliance and financial-reporting activity in Australia; capacity constraints here can ripple into audit timeliness and reporting quality economy-wide.
insights.quote: Oxford Economics Australia estimates that the accounting profession contributed $82.4 billion to Australia’s GDP in 2024–25, equivalent to around 3% of the national economy
insights.locator: Oxford Economics Australia estimates that the accounting

insights.claim: Australia's accounting profession supported more than 365,000 jobs in the 2024-25 assessment period.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Establishes the profession's scale as an employment base, useful as a baseline for tracking Australian services-sector labor market trends.

insights.claim: If treated as a standalone industry, Australia's accounting profession would rank as the country's 13th largest industry by gross value added.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Contextualizes the sector's scale against named Australian industries, useful for sizing addressable markets for accounting software, audit tech and professional-services vendors.
insights.quote: If treated as a standalone industry, accounting would rank as Australia’s 13th largest industry by gross value added.
insights.locator: If treated as a standalone industry

insights.claim: More than two-thirds of the Australian accounting profession's economic contribution comes from accountants working in-house outside accounting firms, spread across financial services, mining, construction, manufacturing, healthcare, retail and the public sector.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Most of the profession's economic value sits inside corporates and government finance functions rather than accounting-firm revenue, so any talent shortage will hit corporate finance teams broadly, not just audit/advisory firms.
insights.quote: More than two-thirds of the profession’s economic contribution comes from accountants working outside accounting firms
insights.locator: More than two-thirds of the profession’s economic contribution

insights.claim: Oxford Economics Australia projects Australia's accounting workforce will expand by around 20% by 2035 on continued demand for accounting professionals.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A decade-long 20% headcount growth projection points to sustained hiring demand in accounting and finance roles, relevant for staffing firms, recruiters and finance-function budgeting.
insights.quote: the accounting workforce projected to expand by around 20% by 2035

insights.claim: Despite projected workforce growth, Oxford Economics forecasts a shortfall of 17,900 accounting, audit and finance professionals in Australia by 2035.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A near-18,000-person talent gap by 2035 is a structural risk to audit quality and compliance capacity, and a likely driver of wage inflation in Australian finance and accounting roles.
insights.quote: a projected shortfall of 17,900 accounting, audit and finance professionals by 2035

insights.claim: The projected Australian accounting talent shortfall is being driven by declining education enrolments, workforce attrition, skilled migration constraints, and the changing impact of AI on the profession.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Because the drivers are structural rather than cyclical, the shortfall is unlikely to self-correct quickly, favoring investment in training pipelines, migration policy reform, and AI-augmented productivity tools for finance teams.
insights.quote: Declining education enrolments, workforce attrition, skilled migration constraints and the changing impact of AI are among the factors shaping the profession’s future workforce.

insights.claim: The economic-impact study was commissioned by Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand and conducted by Oxford Economics Australia, covering both the accounting services industry and accountants employed in-house across businesses, government agencies and other organisations.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
entities: Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand
insights.so_what: The commissioning body is the accountants' own professional association, a relevant context for weighing the independence of the workforce-shortfall estimates.
insights.quote: Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand commissioned Oxford Economics Australia to assess the contribution of the accounting profession to Australia’s economy

insights.claim: Michael Brennan, Director of Economic Impact at Oxford Economics and formerly of Accenture Strategy, AlphaBeta and Deloitte Access Economics, is the named expert behind the accounting profession's economic-impact and workforce analysis.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Brennan's background spans energy transition, digital transformation and workforce planning, suggesting Oxford Economics Australia is positioning this workforce/AI-impact study within a broader policy-advisory practice worth watching for follow-on sector reports.
